Madagascar 
1) Madagascar is an island country located off the south eastern coast of Africa. The island is the fourth largest in the world. 
Only Greenland, New Guinea, and Borneo are larger. Madagascar is known as the Great Red Island for its rich, red soil. Its 
capital is Antananarivo.  
2) Madagascar lies in the western India Ocean. The Mozambique Channel separates the island from the African coast. The 
central part of Madagascar is a plateau, or high, flat land. Mountains rise above the plateau in some places. Maromokotro 
Peak in the north is the island’s highest point. It rises 9,436 feet (2,876 meters). A narrow plain runs along the east coast. Low 
plateaus and plains cover the west. Rivers are short and fast flowing in the east and longer in the west. The east coast has a 
hot, humid tropical climate. The central plateau is cooler. The southwest is dry.  
3) Grasses cover most of the island. Some tropical forests and mangrove swamps survive on the coasts. Hundreds of different 
kinds of orchid also grow in Madagascar. Madagascar has many types of animals that live almost nowhere else in the world. 
Two examples are lemurs and fossas. Lemurs are monkeylike animals that live in trees. Fossas are catlike mammals that hunt 
birds and lemurs. Many butterflies, chameleons, and crocodiles also live in the country.  
4) Madagascar’s people are known as the Malagasy. The Malagasy are more closely related to Indonesians than to Africans, 
even though the country is closer to Africa than to Indonesia. The Malagasy are divided into about 20 groups. The Merina 
make up the largest group. The country also has small groups of people from Africa, Asia, France, and the nearby island 
country of Comoros. Many people of Madagascar speak both the Malagasy and French languages. About half of the people are 
Christian, and most of the rest follow traditional Malagasy religions. Fewer than one-third of the people live in cities. Almost 
all the major cities and towns are in the east. 5) Madagascar is a poor country. Most of the people live by growing crops and by 
raising humped cattle called zebu. Rice is the main food crop. Farmers grow vanilla and cloves to sell to other countries. Vanilla 
from Madagascar is thought to be the best in the world. Madagascar also produces coffee, sugar, and shrimp. Madagascar's 
small industries make mainly cloth, clothing, cement, soap, beer, and cigarettes. Mines provide cobalt, chromite, graphite, 
gold, and gems. Cobalt is the main product. The country's share of world cobalt sales was nearly 4% in 1980. 6) People first 
came to Madagascar from Indonesia more than 1,100 years ago. Arab sailors arrived on the island in AD 1000. The Portuguese 
first came to Madagascar in 1500, and the French arrived and set up small towns so they could trade in the 1600s. The 
Malagasy Merina kingdom controlled much of the island in the early 1800s. The French defeated the Merina in 1895. France 
then ruled the island as a colony. The island became the independent Malagasy Republic in 1960. In the 1970s, the country's 
army took power. The country took the name Madagascar in 1975. In 1992, Madagascar held free elections for the first time in 
17 years. The new government is working to improve the economy.

at restaurants, fast food is usually sold at grocery stores and gas stations. Examples of this include hotdogs, meat pies, and

food that may not be so well known. Some examples of these include kebabs, Chinese takeaways (fried noodles, rice and meat 
dishes), sushi and bento type foods in Japan and fish and chips in the UK, New Zealand and Australia.

Brazil’s water shortage: São Paulo suffers its worst drought on record 
1) Brazil continues to suffer from a historic drought (lack of water), and millions of people in its largest city might run out of 
water soon. São Paulo, home to around 20 million people, is experiencing its lowest rainfall since 1930, and new water-saving 
measures have been introduced to deal with such a very difficult situation. 90% of people in São Paulo say that they are being 
affected by the water shortage. People in other cities such as Rio Janeiro with 7 million people and the capital city of Brasilia 
with 5 million people are not experiencing the same problems that are happening in São Paulo.  
2) Services, including schools and hospitals, are having to adapt to the country's new water problems. The Cândido Fontoura 
children's hospital has denied that it ran out of water earlier this month, but biologist Analice Dora expressed fear: "Everyone 
is worried. Hospitals are the one place that can't lack water." If there is not enough water in hospitals, people could die 
because they cannot get medical treatments. Water is important to hospitals because it is important for the area to be clean.  
3) Although there has been a recent increase in rainfall in the region, it hasn't been enough to improve supply in Brazil, a 
country which normally has 12 per cent of the world's freshwater – more water than any other country in the world. 4) current 
reserves in São Paulo stand at just 10 per cent—known as the "dead volume"—and the government has warned that it could 
get worse in the next few months. Reserves are the water that is stored or kept. This is usually used in cases of emergencies. 
5) Professor Decio Semensatto from the Federal University of São Paulo has compared the current water situation to a "semi-
desert." And the water crisis will probably last for years. He says that water utility Sabesp is responsible because it has known 
for years that drought-like conditions would soon arrive, but did not do much to prevent the future problems. The current 
crisis has reached a serious point, and water rationing may be necessary. Rationing is where only small amounts of something 
are available. People will only be able to get small amounts of water and will have to use it for only things that are very 
important. São Paulo State governor Geraldo Alckmin last month admitted that it was already happening. Brazil is not used to 
such scarcity, but São Paulo is getting used to the way things have to run; There are incentives to use less water, fines for 
those who use too much and the possible installation of more efficient taps. Sabesp will see if such steps can make the 
difference before it decides whether to formally introduce wider water rationing. President Bolsonaro has not done anything 
to help resolve the problem. He does not think that it is a problem for the federal government to solve and has said that the 
local government needs to fix the problem.

Passage 5 
The Aral Sea 
1) The Aral Sea is a large lake located in the former Soviet Union (today's Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan). It was once a beautiful 
lake, surrounded by trees. It supported a large population of fishermen and farmers, but now living near the Aral Sea is 
difficult. The fishing industry is almost gone, and farming is impossible.  
2) In the 1950s, the Soviet government started several huge national agricultural projects in the region around the Aral Sea. It 
wanted to produce cotton for export. It extracted the water needed to produce this valuable crop from the rivers that feed the 
Aral Sea. This was good for the national economy, but terrible for the region. First, the climate around the Aral Sea changed. 
The land next to a large body of water tends to be warmer in the winter and cooler in the summer than land that is not near 
water. By 1990, the Aral Sea had lost 60% of its volume and had halved in the area. Due to this change, summers in the area 
became hotter and winters colder. Second, the government farms used harmful chemicals that were bad for the environment. 
These caused the water to become toxic, killing fish and making it more difficult to get clean drinking water. The worst effect, 
however, has been on public health. In summer, when the Aral Sea dries up, the wind blows toxic sand into towns causing 
several serious health problems including asthma, cancer, and diabetes.

Red flags that a text is spam 
1) It appears unexpectedly. If your “bank” sends you a random text, asking for some action on your part, and it doesn’t come 
from a regular source or at an expected time, check for an accompanying email and call the customer service number listed on 
the official website to confirm.  
2) It makes little sense. If the message has spelling and grammatical errors, or the vocabulary doesn’t seem a bit wrong, then 
it’s either from your six year-old nephew, or most likely it’s spam.  
3) It contains a strange link. Spam texts often contain a link. Sometimes that link appears to lead to a legitimate site, but on 
closer inspection, a critical word or letter is missing or misspelled. For example, “amazon.com” could become something like 
“amzon.com”  
4) It leads to mean calls. If you reply to a spam text or open a link, they may follow up by calling you. if you don’t ever get a call 
from a “customer service representative” who makes you feel perplexed, as if you don’t know why they are calling, hang up.

Public Libraries 
1) As online learning becomes more common and more resources are converted to digital form, some local governments 
suggest that public libraries should be shut down and, in their place, everyone should be given an iPad with an e reader 
subscription.  
2) Proponents of this idea believe that it will save local cities and towns money because libraries are actually expensive to 
maintain. Libraries require a lot of land and real estate to house various books and resources, which makes it somewhat 
expensive to maintain. They also think it will encourage more people to read because they won't have to travel to a library to 
get a book; they can simply click on what they want to read and read it from wherever they are. They could also access more 
materials because libraries won't have to buy physical copies of books; they can simply rent out as many digital copies as they 
need.  
3) However, it would be a serious mistake to replace libraries with tablets. Digital books and resources are associated with less 
learning and more problems than print resources. A study done on tablet versus book reading found that people read 20-30% 
slower on tablets, retain 20% less information, and understand 10% less of what they read compared to people who read the 
same information in print. Additionally, staring too long at a screen has been shown to cause blurred vision, dizziness, dry 
eyes, headaches, and eye strain, at much higher instances than reading print does. People who use tablets and mobile devices
625 
excessively also have a higher incidence of more serious health issues such as fibromyalgia, shoulder and back pain, and 
muscle strain.  
4) While replacing libraries with tablets may seem like a simple solution, it would encourage people to spend even more time 
looking at digital screens, despite the myriad issues surrounding them. It would also end access to many of the benefits of 
libraries that people have come to rely on. In many areas, libraries are such an important part of the community network that 
they could never be replaced by a simple object.

working style to the obvious talent of some players. The four-time Asian champions are in a very good place at the moment.
